newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: Price stability serves society - NZ central bank.
newsitem.headline: Price stability serves society - NZ central bank.

text.p: New Zealand's central bank has moved to reassure the public that its aims of price stability and low inflation build a more just society.
In a booklet published on Monday, Reserve Bank Governor Don Brash said the essence of price stability was to protect people's savings and incomes.

"I believe that price stability... encourages investment in the nation's productive capacity, thereby contributing to employment, growth, export competitiveness and a more just society," he wrote in the booklet entitled 'The impact of monetary policy on people'.
Brash, appointed in 1988, has overseen a dramatic move down in New Zealand's inflation rate from over 15 percent in 1985 to a level consistently under three percent since 1991.
In the pamphlet he argued strongly against the view that a monetary policy focused on price stability could serve only business interests.
"This booklet dispels that myth," the bank said.
Brash wrote that in reality, inflation hit hardest those with limited or fixed incomes or with small, unsophisticated savings schemes.
"By contrast, wealthy people and companies can easily escape the effects of inflation or even profit from it."
Brash said that if inflation were to promote employment he would favour it.
However, he believed that although unexpected inflation could temporarily boost employment, when wages caught up nothing durable could be gained.

He rejected the perception that the Reserve Bank required unemployment to keep inflation down, saying the bank wanted the sustainable level of employment to be as high as possible as unemployment had personal, social and economic costs.
Brash said the best contribution the bank could make to cutting unemployment was to keep delivering price stability.
"Once that is done, it is other policies, which the Reserve Bank cannot control, that decide unemployment rates."
The governor said there was no causal link between price stability, once achieved, and unemployment or social distress.
"Indeed, the reverse tends to be true. Maximising employment is assisted by having the economy operate as productively as possible and price stability helps this."
"Social distress is certainly not a requirement of price stability or an inevitable consequence."
Those on society's margins were hurt by boom-bust cycles.
High real interest rates in New Zealand reflected strong demand and the failure of New Zealanders to increase their savings significantly, he argued.
Brash rejected suggestions that the Reserve Bank was collaborating in helping to scrap the welfare state in favour of an extreme free-market.
"Price stability is perfectly compatible with either a pure free-market society or a high level of state intervention to promote social equity," Brash said.
"Justice is not served by arbitrary transfers of wealth from those on modest or fixed incomes to those able to make speculative investments, as often occurs with inflation.
"Justice is served by an economy that rewards productive efforts and protects the values of people's savings," he said.
